newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces legal challenge over daughter's role.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces legal challenge over daughter's role.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin is in danger of being taken to court over his decision to appoint his daughter as an official adviser, even though it merely confirms a role she has played for more than a year.

A spokeswoman for Russia's supreme court said on Wednesday that a private citizen had filed a suit against the appointment of Tatyana Dyachenko on the grounds of alleged illegal nepotism. The Kremlin has dimissed the accusations.
Dyachenko, at 37 the younger of Yeltsin's two daughters, first came to the fore more than a year ago when she helped organise her father's successful re-election campaign.

Her role as image-maker became apparent in the glimpses of her at her father's side -- combing his thick white hair or telling his bodyguards they would look less like thugs if they took off their sunglasses.

The only prominent woman in the overwhelmingly male Kremlin court, she has had only one official engagement on her own. But she became more prominent during Yeltsin's heart illness last year, despite keeping the public guessing over her role.
"I'll always work for him in whatever capacity he says," she told the commercial NTV channel last November in the Central Clinical Hospital where Yeltsin underwent cardiac surgery.

Kremlin officials have publicly played down her influence. But on Monday, shortly after the appointment was annouced, she lifted the veil, saying her new job was designed to put an end to ambiguity over her position.
"There are some unpleasant things which it's easy only for me to tell him," Dyachenko told Russian reporters, hinting at the isolation of the powerful leaders everywhere.

And in a comment which will rankle with those who feel she already has undue influence, she added candidly, "...there are probably smarter and professional people around, but it's more convenient for him."

Last year commentators speculated that the Kremlin was playing down Tatyana's influence over her father because his illness made him vulnerable to accusations that he was not making decisions himself.
Along with Anatoly Chubais, then chief of Yeltsin's administration, she was widely thought to have had a hand in a purge of Kremlin hardliners just before the second round of the presidential poll.

Nikolai Yegorov, Yeltsin's Kremlin chief of staff until July, was one of those hardliners. "The only person to whose opinion he listened was his younger daughter Tatyana," he told Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper.

"They needed a person best positioned to influence Yeltsin. And she was the best candidate. They urged her -- 'It would be very good if Dad...' She would go and get the necessary decision," Yegorov said.
Now Yeltsin clearly feels there is little doubt he is in control and Chubais, now hugely influential First Deputy Prime Minister, said last month that Tatyana had a unique role.

"Tatyana Borisovna, in my view, was then and still is a representative of common sense in the high-level power structures," he told the Kommersant daily newspaper, dismissing speculation that he was romantically involved with her.

Little is known about Tatyana's private life. She has two sons, one of whom is called Boris and studies at an exclusive school in Britain. She told NTV this week that she and her husband live with Yeltsin, mainly at a residence outside Moscow.

A trained mathematician, Tatyana worked on the Russian space programme until 1994 when she joined a commercial bank based in the Ural mountains. The bank lost its licence to operate on Monday, the Central Bank said.
Yeltsin's parliamentary foes lost little time in condemning Tatyana's appointment.

The Kremlin responded to their allegations of illegal nepotism by saying that the civil service code in question did not apply. But the row may continue, especially if the Supreme Court decides the suit filed by 25-year-old Moscow lawyer Yuri Samsonov is worthy of a hearing.
